lesson.title: When More Comes with More: Positive Association in Depth
lesson.summary: Explore positive association in depth, including a worked example and an important warning about mistaking correlation for causation, using the classic ice cream and drowning example.
lesson.body:
A positive association is the specific case of direction of association in which the response variable tends to increase as the explanatory variable increases. It is the most intuitive relationship to picture: more of one thing tends to accompany more of the other. Formally, whenever tracing a scatterplot from left to right shows the point cloud generally rising, you are looking at a positive association.

The study hours and exam score example is a clean illustration: (1, 68), (2, 72), (3, 75), (4, 80), (5, 84), (6, 90). Every additional hour of studying in this data set comes paired with a higher score than the previous entry, so the relationship is positive. Notice that the increases are not perfectly identical each time, jumping by 4, 3, 5, 4, and then 6 points, but the overall trend is unmistakably upward, which is all that positive direction requires. A positive association does not demand that every single step be identical, only that the general tendency moves in the same direction.

Positive associations show up constantly outside the classroom. Consider a small sample of five houses: as square footage goes from 1000 to 1200 to 1500 to 1800 to 2000, sale price rises from roughly 150,000 to 175,000 to 210,000 to 240,000 to 265,000 dollars. Bigger houses cost more, on average, which is exactly the pattern a positive association describes, and it is the kind of relationship a real estate agent relies on informally every day.

A positive association is a statement about a pattern in data, not a statement about cause and effect, and mixing up the two is one of the most common statistical errors. A frequently cited example: monthly ice cream sales and the number of drowning incidents both tend to rise and fall together across the year, showing a clear positive association, yet nobody seriously believes ice cream causes drowning. Both variables are driven by a third, lurking variable, warm weather, which increases both swimming and ice cream purchases at the same time. Positive association only tells you that two variables move together, it never by itself explains why.

Later in this course, the correlation coefficient will give positive association a precise numerical signature: whenever the linear relationship between two quantitative variables is positive, the correlation coefficient r comes out as a positive number between 0 and 1, with values closer to 1 describing a tighter, more consistent positive pattern. For now, it is enough to recognize the shape by eye, since the arithmetic of r simply confirms what a well-drawn scatterplot already shows.

Recognizing positive association is often the first real insight a data set offers. It tells you where to look for potential explanatory factors, even before you have any tools to test whether the relationship is strong, linear, or causal. That is exactly why direction, starting with the positive case, is the first descriptive step in analyzing any new scatterplot.
